newsitem.title: USA: New finance technology has risks -Boston Fed chief.
newsitem.headline: New finance technology has risks -Boston Fed chief.

text.p: - Central banks must ensure that new technology does not threaten the safety of financial services, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Cathy Minehan said on Thursday.

New technology has allowed an array of non-banks to join the financial services field, raising questions about risks involved with non-regulated entities, Minehan told the Chicago Fed's Conference on Bank Structure and Competition
Minehan said the Fed "can and should play a central role" in assessing the risks associated with new technology while guaranteeing stability in the financial services sector.

"How can central banks ensure the safety of the financial system when technological changes that create broadened access, lower costs, new national and international linkages and the potential for unauthorized access or large-scale fraud?" she asked.

"If the public loses confidence that the provision of financial services will be safe and certain, the risks of instability rules, the viability of the banking system is in jeopardy, and ultimately even the soundness of the currency is at risk," Minehan cautioned.
She noted the issue of whether to put non-banks under the umbrella of regulators such as the Fed has not been settled yet.
"Technology even threatens the very definition of the money supply. Stored-value cards, software-based electronic transfer systems begin to offer value-transfer capability," she said.
However, Minehan also noted the positive developments associated with new technologies that allow for better and better-priced financial services.
"Real problems appear in the failure of old-fashioned controls," she said.
"A central bank needs to be sensitive to the manner in which new technologies are used to provide financial services." However, she said "New regulations may well be misguided right now."

She said "Central banks need to understand how major new financial services are being provided and how to rule, control and participate in such services." Minehan stressed the need for cooperation between the private sector and regulators.
Minehan noted a central bank must protect the value of the currency, provide financial stability and "ensure the economic system is served by a strong and viable banking system."
"Central banks cannot perform these tasks without a deep and abiding concern over how financial services are provided," Minehan said.
